sections.title: Elevator Pitch
sections.dek: A dark-medieval sandbox MMO whose history is written entirely by the players.

hero.alt: Stillmarch logo: a four-pointed compass star inside a bronze circle, beside the wordmark STILLMARCH

blocks.text: Stillmarch is a dark-medieval, open-world sandbox MMO built on PvP, building, crafting, and politics. There is no main quest and no NPC king telling anyone what to do — the server's history is written entirely by the players: alliances, betrayals, who took which region from whom, and when.
Reference points the developer named directly: Albion, Lineage 2, EVE, and Pax Dei.

The developer is explicit this is a passion project, not an attempt at “WoW 2.0,” and that he's deliberately avoiding an Ashes of Creation–style situation — announcing a hundred systems and shipping only a tenth. The scope is large, but design centers on a small number of systems that all interlock.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.dek: The demo cheatsheet: keys, and the first hours from pebbles to a settlement.

blocks.caption: Keys
rows: Free cursor — menus, clicking on people
Basic attack of the weapon in hand
Drop the item under the cursor

blocks.text: The first hours

items: Make money first: pebbles, sticks and herbs lie all over the ground around the Wayfarer Village and need no tools. Sell them at the Crown orders board next to the mint.
Make tools: stick + stone hand recipes give crude tools — hatchet, pickaxe, sickle, knife. Put them in the TOOLS slots.
Gather raw materials, have workshop NPCs process them, and craft (or buy) gear at the player benches — see Crafting, Gathering & Materials.

Fight with whatever weapon you like — the weapon in your hand is your class. Wolves and deer are the easy start; the skeleton guards (the Forgotten) at the four strongholds hit hard — bring a group or a healer.
Keep Focus above 75% for +10% XP; carry a lantern at night.
Settle down: a House leader claims an Obelisk and builds a settlement on the claim grid (N). Talk to people — most of the economy is other people's needs.

blocks.text: Source: the demo cheatsheet handed to players. It isn't dated and likely predates action.20: it places the skeleton guards at the watchtowers, which action.20 rebuilt as four strongholds — updated to strongholds here.

New characters start in a Castaway tunic and shorts, given once when you pick your starting village. A first weapon can be made by hand: a Wooden Training Sword or Longsword (Woodworking 1) from sticks and a scrap of cloth (see Crafting → Tier 0 & quality caps).

sections.title: Setting & Lore
sections.dek: Valdris, a thousand years after the Stillness.

hero.alt: The Stillmarch emblem: a steel compass star with a glowing blue core, framed by a bronze circle

blocks.text: The continent is called Valdris. A thousand years ago the empire Perpetua united it, ended every war, and declared history finished.
Then came the Stillness — not an invasion or a plague, but a slow cultural collapse: people simply stopped finishing things. Within a few years the whole continent went silent.

The only people who escaped by ship were the ones still capable of friction and unfinished business: debtors, heretics, sailors, prisoners. Players are their descendants, returning after a thousand years with nothing — no books, no records, no time to pack.
What's left behind

items: Obelisks — machines left behind by Perpetua that nobody alive understands. Players light Obelisks that aren't theirs and build villages around them.
The Forgotten — Perpetua's soldiers, still walking their patrols in old watchtowers, because a patrol has no defined end and nobody ever told them to stop.
The Blight — spreads outward from Forgotten-held sites. Color drains from the land, wood starts behaving like stone, and animals there aren't sick, just confused.

blocks.text: Remember shame rather than remember nothing.
blocks.cite: Returner custom — Returners write everything down, including their own betrayals

blocks.text: Tradition: every player-built building has one small detail left deliberately unfinished, for reasons nobody can explain.
Overall tone: a world winding down, carried by a small, stubborn, possibly unjustified hope that this time civilization holds.

sections.title: Houses, Baronies, Kingdoms & Empires
sections.dek: The guild unit is a House — part family, part company, with no preset class.

blocks.text: There's no pre-selected “guild type.” What a House is comes from what its members actually do week to week, not a checkbox at creation. Specialization is dynamic — stop running the banks and you stop being a banking House.

blocks.caption: House archetypes (emergent, not chosen)
rows: Holds Obelisks, walls, and a castle; lives off land and taxes.
Runs loans and letters of credit; can fund or cut off anyone.
Runs trade routes along the roads.
Builds a temple, runs its own faith and followers.
Keeps barracks, sells its blades to whichever side pays — can work both sides of a war.
Lives off robbery on the roads, flying a bandit's flag.

blocks.text: Scaling structure

items: A House holding 3 regions becomes a barony.
Baronies allied under an elected king (elections every 4 weeks; no single barony can hold more than 30% of the vote) form a kingdom.
Allied kingdoms form an empire — the server is only expected to support 2–3 empires at once.
The crown is borrowed, never owned.

blocks.text: Regions vs Houses

items: An Obelisk isn't the House: the House just rules the region.
Anyone can become a citizen of a region by clicking a button on its Obelisk, and anyone can rent a plot — plots in a village don't have to be House-owned.
Regions will have NPCs tied to the region itself, such as NPC guards, which are also hired (see Wayfarers & NPC Workers).

blocks.text: House crest (0.5.0)

items: A new crest creator: 20 field divisions and any colour from an RGB picker, instead of a few fixed tinctures.
64 charges in four groups — classic, beasts, objects, symbols — 48 of them new.
Up to 3 layers of charges. Each can be moved, scaled, rotated, mirrored and repeated in heraldic layouts. A charge stays where you put it instead of dropping to the bottom of the shield.
Crests look painted on wood on shields, and like cloth on banners and standards.
Your crest shows on the Claim Banner, the claim camp standard, the world map, and in the House and region windows.
The banner's flag waves more calmly and follows the in-game wind, no longer clips into the wooden pole, and the crest on it is no longer squashed.

blocks.text: Betrayal is built into the culture: it gets written into the Chronicles, and in some Houses is considered an honor rather than a shame.

sections.title: Combat
sections.dek: Crosshair-aimed action combat where the animation is the clock.

blocks.text: Base kit: action combat, crosshair aiming, not tab-target. Five weapon stances — sword & shield, greatsword, staff, bow, and bare hands — each with distinct animations and skills.
Basic attack commit & combos

items: The animation is the clock: a hit lands exactly at the clip's contact frame; the next swing can only start once the current swing ends. The server enforces the same timing, so client and server agree on what landed.
Direction locks at the start of the swing — turning only returns during recovery. Movement speed during a swing drops to 70%.

Combo chains: clicking inside the “chain window” starts the next swing immediately; clicking earlier buffers the input; holding LMB keeps swinging without dropping to idle. Chains use real combo variants (sword A1→A2→A3; greatsword A1→A2→A3_B); the last swing in a chain is a finisher at x1.3 damage. The crosshair ring lights up when the chain window is open.

Root motion on basics: the character moves exactly as animated during a swing (no artificial forward step); the server plays the identical variant so other players see the same thing you do. A swing now stops at the target instead of pushing through it.
Legs no longer slide while swinging on the move — the swing plays on the upper body, legs are driven by locomotion separately (extended to skills in action.20).
Dodge (Alt) during a basic's recovery now works correctly — the dodge impulse was previously getting lost under the animation.
Block (RMB) pressed during a swing's active window now waits for recovery before engaging, same as dodge.
Staff: Holy Bolt runs on the same commit system — a 3-variant chain with a finisher; you can shoot while moving (50% movement slow while casting).
Bow: Quick Shot uses the same swing-window system as melee weapons; you can shoot while moving without leg-sliding.
Hit sounds are quieter and throttled to at most once every 0.4s per target, so a rapid combo no longer thuds on a repetitive loop.

Buff/debuff replication rewritten: effect state (Sunder, bleed, slow, stun, Stagger, Bone Wall, taunt, mob casting) is now correctly replicated per-character — fixed a bug where you could see debuff icons on players who didn't actually have that debuff.

blocks.text: Skill commit & spin attacks

items: Basic ↔ skill commit: a basic pressed during a skill waits for the skill to end; a skill pressed during a basic swing waits for the chain window.
The chain window opens 0.2s before the end of every swing — a click inside it is rewarded with an immediate follow-up, a held LMB waits until the swing ends.
Spin attacks — Great Sweep, Rend, Shattering Sweep, Execute — play on the full body with a movement lock.
Great Sweep deals its damage in 3 portions during the spin and shows a channel bar.
Skills cast while moving play on the upper body — legs come from locomotion, no sliding.
Clicking right after a skill no longer fires a basic attack with no animation — the attack waits until the skill ends.
Holding LMB to attack no longer makes your character snap at the start of each swing.
Sweeping Cleave deals 2.5× more damage.
A basic staff attack while moving plays on the upper body and your legs keep walking — you can shoot on the move.
The staff's third combo hit now matches the rest — it came from a different animation set.

blocks.text: Healing & support

items: T cycles through allies to heal — party first, alive before dead. The cast bar names the target: “Holy Mending → Name”, or “Self”.
Target too far: an instant heal is refused before the cast; a cast-time heal lands on you instead and shows a warning. Party frames flash red with “Too far”.
Heals and buffs only work on allies — party and House members — never on enemies. (Widened in 0.6.6 — see Open-world PvP below.)

blocks.text: Fixed, action.20: the HoT (Renew) kept healing noticeably longer than its buff icon's counter showed — the kit's clock mixed real time with game time, and refreshing the buff stacked a second tick loop. It now ends together with its icon.
Block & guard

items: RMB, melee weapons only. Holding RMB raises your guard; a block bar appears above the cast bar.
Block pool = weapon Block Rating + shield Block Rating, shown on the item tooltip and character panel.
Holding the block slowly drains the pool on its own; every frontal hit drains its damage from the pool, and only 30% of that hit's damage still gets through to you.
Guard break: pool hits empty → 6 seconds with no blocking and no pool regeneration. Release the block and the pool regenerates passively over time.
Block only covers the front arc (±65°), slows movement to 60%, and locks out skills while held. Dodging (Alt) drops your guard immediately.
Dedicated guard-up animations for sword & shield and greatsword; a blocked hit sparks and rings, a guard break plays a parry animation.
Blockable: sweeps and cones, including the skeleton Heavy Blow. Not blockable: ground-effect abilities — Rain of Arrows, Ground Slam, Radiance, the Iron Vigil aura, and bleeds.

blocks.text: Guard responsiveness: the guard rises the instant RMB is pressed (no longer waiting for server replication) and ×2.2 faster; releasing RMB lowers the shield at once.
Holding your guard while nobody hits you drains the pool half as fast.
Fixed, action.19: blocking with a sheathed weapon previously let you guard bare-handed — now blocking properly draws the weapon first, like attacking does.
Melee basics (arc hits)
Basic swings hit every enemy in a cone in front of you, crosshair-aimed (your body turns into the swing), up to 8 targets.
Weapon reach was cut to match the length of the blade.

items: Dodge (Alt) shows a small white cooldown bar under the crosshair; the dodge icon was removed from the skill bar.
Character panel has Attack Speed and Block Rating rows.

blocks.text: Fixed, action.17: hitting multiple enemies at once previously only showed 2 damage numbers, due to an engine RPC cap.
Balance tuning (post-21 Sept playtest)

items: Fervor: a hit taken now gives 50% less Fervor; Fervor starts draining 7s after the last exchange of damage (was ~18s in action.17) — much faster drain onset.
Player HP x1.5: base HP 200 → 300, and every armor HP bonus is also x1.5 — a direct response to PvP time-to-kill feeling too short.
Weapon tiers strengthened: Tier 3 weapons deal x2.05 of Tier 1 damage, Tier 4 weapons deal x2.9 of Tier 1 damage.
Mob respawn standardized to 30 minutes, including mobs running their own separate copy of stats.

blocks.text: Balance & feedback (0.4.2)

items: Battle Surge removed: the first hit of a fight no longer gives bonus Fervor.
Life leech shows as healing numbers.

blocks.text: 0.5.0 changes

items: In action mode your basic attack goes for the enemy in front of the camera (20° cone); the ring shows the chosen target.
A basic attack cuts off a skill's animation once the skill has taken effect, so you don't wait for it to finish — only casts are protected. (Since action.20 a basic had waited for the whole skill.)
A dodge plays out fully (0.6 s). Skills pressed during it fire after it instead of cutting it short.
Taunt has a targeting mode: the first key press shows an arrow over the enemy (red in range, grey too far); a second press or LMB throws it, RMB cancels.
Shield Charge runs up to the target, and the damage and stun land on arrival.
Wide Slash no longer jerks your character and camera.
The staff stays planted while it releases a spell instead of sliding.
The sword's first combo hit is slower — it was too fast.
Stunned mobs really stand still: they don't shoot, turn or walk, and humans play a stunned animation.
Damage numbers no longer flash for a frame in the top-left corner of the screen.

blocks.text: 0.5.3 changes

items: When an enemy hit you, two numbers popped up: the raw damage and the damage after armour. Now there's one — the real one.
A blocked hit shows “N Blocked” in steel blue, where N is the damage that got through. Before, the number looked like an unblocked hit even though you lost less HP.
The same bug counted Fervor from monster hits, and cast pushback, twice. Both now count once.

blocks.text: Staff & resources (0.5.3)

items: The staff basic attack deals half the damage. It out-damaged the two-handed sword and let you keep moving.
New sprint animation with the staff, without the “angry” forward lean.
The Lumen bar no longer disappears at zero: an empty bar pulses so you can see you're out.
With a staff in hand you always see Lumen — before, the bar sometimes switched to Fervor.
T2–T4 staves get the larger Lumen pool like T1, and T2–T4 swords (one-handed, two-handed, longsword) get the Fervor bonus like T1. The bonuses used to apply to T1 only.

blocks.text: Archer (0.6.0)

items: Aim with RMB and draw with LMB. The crosshair closes as the string tightens and lights up at full draw.
New bow model, new movement with the bow in hand, and new draw, aim and release animations. The bow sits properly on your back.
New skill, Hawk's Descent (35 Fervor, 60 s cooldown): leap 9 m up, hover for up to 5 seconds and shoot talon arrows from above. Use it again to come down early.
The bow bar changes: Aimed Shot is gone, Crippling Shot unlocks at bow level 2 and Hawk's Descent at level 3. Rain of Arrows and Piercing Volley stay at 4 and 6.

Bow skills have their own effects instead of smoke and explosions. Piercing Volley fires 5 arrows with thick trails; Rain of Arrows sends a volley into the sky, then 18 arrows stick into the ground, and its damage lands together with the arrows.
Crippling Shot slows monsters reliably, leaves an icy trail and frosts the target's feet while the slow lasts.
New bow sounds — see Sound.

blocks.text: 0.6.0 changes

items: A blocked hit shows two numbers: the damage you took, and “N Blocked” for what your guard stopped. (In 0.5.3 a single “N Blocked” showed the damage that got through.)

Gear wears out: weapons with every hit you land, armour and shields with every hit you take. A broken weapon deals no damage and broken armour gives no protection (see Crafting → Durability & repair).
Dying costs 25% durability on everything you wear.

blocks.text: 0.6.5 changes

Far fewer movement corrections (rubber-banding). Dodge, Hawk's Leap (Hawk's Descent in the 0.6.0 notes) and the block pushback are predicted on your side and confirmed by the server in the same move; slows and stuns apply in step with your movement; and the stamina checks for sprint and jump match between your game and the server. The server also accepts small position differences.
Open-world PvP (0.6.6)

items: Outside safe zones you can damage any player who isn't in your party or warband. Your House and alliance no longer protect you from damage: accidentally hitting one of your own is on you and your reputation.

Aggression flag: attacking a player lights a flag for 2 minutes. The attacker and the victim with their party then see each other in red, and auto-targeting picks them up. Every further hit refreshes the flag, and the game shows a message about it.
In a siege, players on the same side of the declaration can't hurt each other.
Single-target heals work on your party, warband, House, allies and residents of your region, but not on strangers. Group heals still only cover your party or warband.
Auto-targeting only picks enemies and flagged players among other players, so it no longer jumps to random passers-by.

blocks.caption: Names, nameplates and the target ring are coloured by relation (0.6.6)
rows: Only an enemy House at war, or a player with an aggression flag

blocks.text: Residents take no PvP damage within 12 m of their region's Obelisk, except while it's under attack, and drop no loot when they die in their own town (see Building & Logistics → Resident towns).
Weapon tier unlocks skills (0.6.8)
A lower-tier weapon unlocks only part of its skills. The basic attack and dodge always work, and skills unlock in the same order as they do with weapon level.

blocks.caption: Skills a weapon unlocks by its tier (0.6.8)

items: One-handed weapons unlock fewer because your other hand holds a second weapon. A shield counts by its own tier.
A weapon in the highest tier that exists for its type unlocks everything. Today that's the bow: it only exists as T1, so archers keep all their skills.
A locked skill is dimmed on the action bar with a padlock, and its tooltip says “Requires a Tier N weapon”. The skills window (K) shows the tier needed (“T2”) instead of a level.
The weapon tooltip says how many skills it unlocks, e.g. “Weapon skills: 2 of 5 · Tier 2 unlocks 4”.

blocks.text: 0.6.9 changes
Monster arrows no longer kick up a dust puff when they hit.
General design notes

items.text: Weapon-based leveling: each weapon has its own level/XP, including the offhand (a shield levels separately from the main-hand weapon).

No classes — the weapon in your hand is your class: sword & shield = tank, two-hander = damage, staff = healer, bow = ranged. At weapon level 1 you only have the basic attack; each level unlocks one skill (K shows skills and weapon levels). Since 0.6.8 the weapon's tier also limits how many skills it unlocks (see above).
Heavy armour protects more but slows you down. The weapon tooltip shows Attack Speed.
Dying leaves your body where you fell: a staff user can resurrect you, otherwise you respawn at the graveyard.
Individual skill trees per weapon are planned.

Commitment mechanic (basics commit you to the swing's direction/animation, no canceling mid-swing) was chosen after reviewing New World combat footage, aiming for a middle ground between New World (fast, weighty, laggy at scale) and Pax Dei (slower-paced).

Resources: Fervor (rage, physical weapons) and Lumen (mana, magic weapons) — only the relevant bar shows depending on equipped weapon; dual-resource loadouts are planned. Guard and Stamina also exist; Stamina is hidden by default.
Resource cost tuning: Lumen ability costs +25% (Mending 19, Renewal 25, Blessing 31, Resurrect 63, Combat Res 100); Fervor generation −40% (further reduced again in action.19).
Action bar: roughly 8–10 spell slots plus extra consumable/item slots.
Damage/healing numbers should only display for the player, not allies/party; drop the “+” on healing numbers; damage numbers slightly smaller.
Partly addressed in action.20: other people's damage numbers are shown at ×0.5 size when they're in your party, and hidden entirely for strangers.
Low HP feedback is still sound only — since 0.4.2 a heartbeat plays below 40% health, heavier and faster below 20% (see Sound) — with no visual indicator yet.
No plans for damage/healing meters — considered too likely to push toward min-maxing.
Party size: 5 players. Since 0.6.6 a warband holds up to 25 (see Party & Player Interaction).
Death penalty: dying drops your entire purse/bag near your corpse; 20% of gold is permanently lost (see Economy).
Crafting/gathering XP was multiplied 10x by the developer to stress-test crafting further.
A weapon left in the helmet slot was incorrectly determining weapon type/animations — now only what's actually in your hands counts.

sections.title: The Forgotten
sections.dek: Perpetua's soldiers, still walking patrols nobody ever ended.

blocks.text: The Forgotten have been buffed twice in two days: once in direct response to players gaining block and area-hit basics (action.17), and again based on 21 Sept playtest feedback (action.19): x2.5 HP and damage over action.17's already-buffed numbers (x4.3 of original base stats overall; armor 70/26).
Hit 50% harder again in action.20: the damage multiplier on basics and skills went from x2.5 to x3.75. HP and armor are unchanged.

In 0.4.2 the normal attacks of the Warrior, Veteran, Patrol and Stalker hit for real damage again — they had been doing 1 damage since 0.3.3. Acolyte bolts now deal their damage when they reach you, not when they are cast.
Strongholds

The eight small watchtower pairs were rebuilt into four large strongholds, one per region: Northreach, Heartland, Eastwood and Southmere. Each stronghold's gate stands at the end of its road and the ground under its walls is levelled. The old watchtower sites are growing back into forest.
Garrisoned again in 0.4.2: from the end of September all four strongholds stood empty, and the only fights were with the camps around them. The thick violet Blight haze is back over them too.

blocks.caption: Garrison per stronghold (action.20)
rows: 1 — alone in the centre of the throne hall

blocks.caption: Enemy roster
rows: Not described yet — first named in 0.4.2
Not described yet — first named in 0.6.5, in Obelisk claim waves

items.text: A built-in halberd-wielding type was removed.
Every watchtower had +3 Forgotten added to its garrison (2 warriors + 1 veteran) — superseded by the action.20 strongholds.
Forgotten use the same animation packs as players — sword & shield / staff stances, strikes, Blight Bolt cast, Heavy Blow, Bone Wall, pounce.
The acolyte's Blight Bolt was resolving as a Heavy Blow (no projectile, no damage) and acolytes were double-casting — both fixed.
The acolyte's Blight Bolt now requires line of sight — it can no longer shoot through dungeon walls.
The Forgotten shriek when they spot you, and let out a hollow cry before they crumble.

Stronghold bosses such as the Ancient Bone Warden drop a Warden Relic 10% of the time — needed for a Claim Banner and for Obelisk level costs (see Territory Control). They also get a big health bar within 30 m.
13 Forgotten in one watchtower were facing the wrong way; they now stand correctly.
The Veteran's area strike (Heavy Blow) winds up for 1.65 s instead of 1.4 s, giving you more time to dodge. The 0.5.3 notes call it the Skeleton Veteran.
The Forgotten can drop a Fragment of the Forgotten Blade, a Relic for weapons (see Crafting → Relics).

blocks.text: Forgotten patrol the Blight Hills biome (see Crafting & Materials).

sections.title: Focus System
sections.dek: XP modifiers that reward staying warmed up.

items: Warrior's Focus and Artisan's Focus are separate meters. High Focus grants bonus XP (combat for Warrior's, crafting/gathering for Artisan's); low Focus applies a penalty.
Focus depletes as you perform the associated actions — long grinding drains it.
Above 75% Focus you earn +10% XP.

blocks.text: In the HUD, a Focus arc next to the HP bar appears only once Focus drops below 75% — i.e. once the bonus is actually gone, since that's the point it's worth knowing about.

items: Higher Craftsman's Focus raises your odds of a better quality when crafting; above 75%, stackable results have a 10% chance of one extra piece (see Crafting → Item quality).
With Combat Focus above 75%, a kill has a 5% chance for an extra rare drop (gems, silver ore).

blocks.text: Naming: the DMs call the meters “Warrior's Focus” and “Artisan's Focus”; the demo cheatsheet calls the crafting one “Craftsman's Focus”, and the 0.6.0 notes use “Combat Focus” and “Craftsman's Focus”.
Planned: player-built taverns will regenerate Focus quickly once it's maxed out, encouraging players to socialize in cities.

sections.title: UI / HUD
sections.dek: Rebuilt in action.19 around a “minimal, contextual” philosophy; refined in action.20 after feedback.

blocks.text: Layout & bars

items: Health, Lumen, and Fervor sit above the action bar (moved off the old top-left corner placement).
HP is visibly thicker, grows in size during combat, and gets a brighter frame plus a crossed-swords icon while in combat.
Numbers display on bars during combat and on hover.
Damage trail: after a hit, a bright segment of the bar lingers briefly before draining out.
Two XP bars run under the action bar at full width — main weapon and shield/offhand — and brighten for 3s after gaining XP; hover shows level and progress.
Focus arcs next to HP appear only below 75% Focus.
Bars never change length, only visibility/emphasis.

blocks.text: Fading / contextual states
The HUD fades out when nothing is happening (calm / ready / combat all exist as states) and returns fully when you draw a weapon, move, acquire a target, or exchange damage.
Buffs, debuffs & nameplates

items: Buff/debuff icons sit directly above the bars: square icons with a burn-down timer frame (gold = buff, red = debuff), debuffs rendered larger. Hover shows name + description; no separate numeric counters.

Nameplates 2.0: party members and allies always show HP + Lumen/Fervor; enemies show HP, and only show Lumen/Fervor when it's not full. An idle mob's name only appears once you're within 35 m. Plates shrink with distance, there's a cap on how many render at once, and target/party/boss plates always show regardless of the cap.

The old target frame in the corner is gone — that information now lives on the nameplate above the target itself. An enemy currently attacking you shows via an aggro badge next to your HP (warning icon + attacker count).

Party mini-frames sit top-left (same margin as chat): name, HP number + bar, a thin Lumen/Fervor bar, the ally's buffs/debuffs, and icons for their equipped weapon and shield. Click a frame to target that player.

blocks.text: Compass, toasts & chat

items: Compass runs along the top: cardinal directions; Obelisks (diamond icon) and settlements (house icon), each showing the nearest one's name and distance; party members (green dot); a living boss nearby (warning icon); your own cart; your last death spot (skull icon). The compass never fades.

Toasts (small popups above the bars) replace chat-line spam for: loot (stacks, e.g. “+2 Bone”), XP gains, warnings (e.g. lantern out of oil, shown with a red frame), and region/workshop messages. Max 3 toasts at once, 4s duration, each with an icon; a copy of every toast is still written to chat as a journal log.
Chat fades after 10s with no new messages, and reappears on a new incoming line or when you start typing (Enter).
“Say” is heard only by players within 40 m of the speaker, and a speech bubble appears above the character, visible up to 25 m.
Build messages (e.g. “Undone”) are tagged [Build] in chat instead of [Region], and only the builder sees them.

blocks.text: Menu & settings

items: All menu icons collapsed into a single button in the bottom-right. Hovering or pressing Tab expands them under the cursor; a second Tab press or clicking an entry collapses it again. Tab no longer toggles the old bare cursor mode.
Map (M): the cart and your last death spot now render as proper icons.

Settings → HUD settings (new panel): HUD visibility profile (Minimal / Full / Auto — Auto hides the whole HUD when calm), bar numbers (in combat / always / hover-only), nameplate mode (default / names always / minimal), compass on/off, interface scale (80–125%), and chat opacity.
Main menu: a new SOUND button holds the volume sliders, and SETTINGS is now called GRAPHICS (see Development & Testing → Video memory & graphics settings).

blocks.text: Visual style

items: Flat bars and plates in a cold-steel palette — no gradient backgrounds, no pack textures or frames (the single font of action.19 was replaced in action.20 — see below).
Resource colors: HP deep red, Lumen amber, Fervor ember.
All HUD icons (menu, compass, map, toasts) now come from a single consistent icon pack.

blocks.text: action.20 revision (after feedback)

items: New fonts: Alegreya Sans for text, Cinzel for numbers, the compass and damage.
Only the active resource is shown (Lumen or Fervor) — on the bars, party frames and nameplates; both return once a weapon uses both.
Bars: HP 16/20 px, resources 9 px, gains animate; Lumen and Fervor numbers are shown separately in their bar colours.
XP bars are only visible for 3s after a gain (or on hover with the cursor), replacing the always-on brighten effect.
Notifications restyled New World–style: item icon in a square, “Looted X ×N”, “+N XP <weapon>”, small 12 px icons, warnings marked with a red “!”.
Cast bar: icon on the left, spell name in small caps, time remaining on the right; channels count down.
The buff countdown ring fades together with the HUD; the aggro badge next to HP lost its background (10 px triangle + attacker count).
Chat no longer wakes up for loot/XP — it's active only while typing and hides after silence. The “Combat” HUD state now triggers only on damage involving you.
Nameplates 2.0 are on by default; the kit's own player plate is collapsed.
Party frames: see Party & Player Interaction.

blocks.text: 0.4.2 changes

items: The banner shown when you enter a region or location is readable: engraved, outlined lettering on a soft dark backdrop. Before, it got lost against a bright sky or fog.
Tab shows your active buffs and debuffs at the bottom of the screen; hover one to read what it does.
The aggro badge is now an eye that pulses gently on a dark glass background, with the attacker count lined up with it. It disappears once the enemy is dead or gives up.
The chat greets you with “Welcome to Stillmarch!” and the current chat commands.

blocks.text: Event HUD & boss bars (0.5.0)

items: One shared layout for claims and bosses: an event card on the right (objectives and time) and a big bar at the top of the screen.
During an Obelisk claim the bar shows control for both sides — blue is your side, red your opponents, labelled “Enemies”. A light on the border shows whether you are gaining or losing.
Bosses in the dungeon and in the world (e.g. the Ancient Bone Warden in the strongholds) get a big health bar with their name, shown as soon as you come within 30 m.
Texts under the bar no longer overlap and stay readable against the sky.

blocks.text: Region / House UI

items: Political map (M key): shows who holds each region, its level, prestige, and whether it contains T4 resources.
House screen 2.0 (G or the House icon): tabs — Overview (crest + holdings), Members, Regions, Bank. House name displays in gold over a member's head instead of a default “<Guild>” placeholder.
Region window 2.0: tabs — Overview / Requisitions / Treasury / Plots / Residents / Upgrade — shown based on the viewer's role (outsider, resident, Castellan, Baron); includes a treasury ledger.
Region windows redone in 0.5.0. The region board keeps upkeep deliveries separate from projects.
The Obelisk window has tabs for the region, residency and plots.
The Castellan's Table (a building piece) opens an officials-only window: treasury, projects, land, people (see Building & Logistics).
Tabs look the same in every window.
Opening the Obelisk window for the first time no longer opens the House window.
Obelisk window tabs no longer flicker when you switch them (the scrollbar keeps its place), and every tab opens at the top.

blocks.text: Items & interface look (0.6.0)

items: New icons for all items, made in one style.
A tier badge (a Roman numeral) sits in the corner of every item that has a tier.
New interface look: darker iron and soot instead of navy blue and gold, with solid panels. Gold now marks only Masterwork items.
Stats in tooltips, at the crafting station and on the character card are shown as icons with numbers instead of sentences.
Item tiles use one mark per meaning: the glow shows quality, the corner badge shows tier, a crack mark shows a broken item, and a small mark shows a Relic.
Durability shows as a thin bar on the item and in the tooltip; you get a warning when something drops below 20%.

blocks.text: Forged-iron windows (0.6.1, dropped in 0.6.7)

items: Backpack, equipment, crafting, loot, trade, cart and settings windows are made of soot-blackened forged iron: a hammered iron band around the edge, left open at the bottom-right corner, and the window name on its own iron plate.
Buttons, search fields, filters and equipment slots are forged iron too. The main action button (Craft, Take All) has an edge that glows like hot iron, brighter when you point at it.
Obelisk, region, castellan, storehouse, map, chronicle and order windows keep their slate-and-gold look.
“Crafted by” in tooltips is grey and no longer blends into the item description.
The character hub (Tab) no longer stops your character — you can walk with any tab open.

The compass shows the three Wayfarer villages — Firstlanding, Fernhollow and Highmoor — as a house icon from anywhere on the map. The nearest village shows its name and distance, like the nearest Obelisk.
The “Crafted by” line in item tooltips is easier to tell apart from the description.
Windows (crafting, backpack, character, regions and so on) are back to the Escape menu look: a semi-transparent background without texture, replacing the forged iron of 0.6.1.
Crafting: the main CRAFT button has an R key (hint on the button). You can rebind it in the controls settings (“Craft (crafting window)”).
Compass directions match the world map. Before, east on the compass was south on the map. The war HUD and the claim death panel use the same directions.
The world map (M) is repainted — see World Geography → Rivers.

blocks.text: Character select & interaction (0.6.8)

items: On character select your character stands in an idle pose instead of a T-pose, and the leftover hat from an old set is gone.
No more multi-second freeze after logging in when your character first appears: its look loads in the background.
Interaction works like New World: the thing you use (a rock, herb, tree or chest) is picked from where you look near your character, not only exactly under the crosshair.
The “F” prompt floats next to the object instead of in the middle of the screen.

blocks.text: The F prompt (0.6.9)

items: Targeting is tighter: a 12° cone instead of 30°. Within arm's reach (2 m) what counts is the direction from your character relative to the camera (±35°), so a sapling at your side no longer steals the beech you're looking at.
The prompt hides while a window is open, such as the planner, instead of showing through it.

A missing tool shows a round badge with the tool's icon in place of [F]: a red ring with a cross when you don't have the tool, a glowing ring with an arrow and the tier when yours is too weak. Before, it only said “needs a hatchet”.
New axe, pickaxe, sickle and knife icons that read at 16 px, and a stronger shadow under the prompt.

blocks.text: Loot window (0.6.0)

items: Loot opens as a grid like your backpack, with items at their real size. The grid grows with the bag and keeps items in place while you take them.
Quality, durability and Relics are visible on loot, and hovering an item shows the full tooltip. A bag with something valuable plays its own sound.

blocks.text: Carried over: UI icons originally sourced from a free itch.io pack (“Line Game Icons Ultimate Collection” by SunGraphica), since consolidated into the single HUD icon pack above; crafting/item icons were screenshots of the in-game item mesh, flagged as needing polish, until 0.6.0 redrew them all in one style. Possible loading hitches tied to world-partition streaming are flagged for investigation, not yet confirmed as a core issue.

sections.title: Sound
sections.dek: Reworked in 0.4.2 and 0.4.3: weapon skills, Lumen casts, player voices, enemy calls, wind, and silence in the Blight.

blocks.text: Combat

items: New sounds for most weapon skills: Sweeping Cleave, Shattering, Sundering, Execute, Rend, Wide Slash, Shield Charge, Shield Bash, ground slams and bow shots.
One-handed swords sound like steel instead of a wooden practice sword.
Your character grunts when swinging a weapon or staff, with a heavier shout on combo finishers and weapon skills.
Jumping has a sound (gear rustle, sometimes a short breath), and your character pants when stamina runs out.
A heartbeat plays at low health: soft below 40%, heavier and faster below 20%.

blocks.text: Enemies & the world

items: Enemies call out when they spot you: the Forgotten shriek, wolves bark, drowners gurgle, bandits shout (men and women).
Dying Forgotten let out a hollow cry before they crumble.
Bandit camps can be heard from a distance — laughs, whistles, mutters — unless they're lying in ambush.
A herd no longer calls all at once, which sounded like an echo.
Skinning has a sound.
The stonemason taps stone instead of ringing a bell, and the saw sounds like one stroke, not two.
Music fades out when you enter the Blight and stays silent there.

blocks.text: Lumen, casts & wind (0.4.3)

items: Lumen without the “bells”: new sounds for casting and hitting with Holy Bolt, healing, blessings and auras, resurrection and the Iron Vigil pulse.

Every skill with a cast time plays a sound for the whole cast — gathering energy for Mending, Blessing and resurrections, embers for Berserker's Fury, a drawn bowstring for Aimed Shot. It fades out when the cast ends or is interrupted.
In sunny weather you can clearly hear the wind.
The annoying bumblebee and hissing grasshopper right next to the player are gone from the meadow.
Taunt has a battle cry (male and female voice) under the shield bash.
Drums sound with the on-screen announcements of an Obelisk claim.
Wolves sound meaner: a deeper voice, a snarl instead of a bark when they attack, new pain and death sounds, and a low growl at rest. The Alpha Wolf is deeper still.
The staff's basic attack crackles with Lumen instead of whistling like a sling.
Bow sounds you can feel: a string crack and a low kick on every shot, separate sounds for each skill, arrow impacts, and a dry “tok” for every arrow that hits, which you hear even from 30 m.
The crafting reveal plays sparks and a sound that grow with the item's quality.
A loot bag with something valuable plays its own sound.
New sounds when an item is finished: a hard hammer strike that grows with quality, up to a full burst for Masterwork and Legendary.
Rare loot has a new sound too.

blocks.text: Settings
The sound settings have an “Other players' voices” slider (50% by default) that sets how loud other players' grunts and shouts are.

items: The volume sliders are also in the main menu, under the new SOUND button.
Your saved volumes apply in the main menu right away — the menu music used to play at full volume until you entered the world.

blocks.text: Earlier sound fixes live with their systems: enemy skill sounds stopped carrying across the whole map in the Friday hotfixes, and hit sounds were made quieter and throttled in action.19 (see Combat).

sections.title: Party & Player Interaction
sections.dek: Targeting, whispering, trading and inviting since action.20; warbands and loot rolls since 0.6.6.

blocks.text: Player menu

items: [F] on a player targets them; holding F opens a menu: Target / Whisper / Trade / Invite to Party / Invite to House.
Right-clicking a party mini-frame (cursor via Tab) opens the same menu, plus Promote / Kick / Leave for the party leader.
Whisper opens chat with “/w Name” already typed.
The party/House invite popup now collapses after Accept/Decline — the cursor no longer stays on screen.
A House invitation opens in the game's own window with the House name, and joining shows a banner with the House crest and who invited you.
Inviting by name no longer cares about upper and lower case.

blocks.text: Party frames

items: C+2…C+5 targets a party member: the targeted frame gets a gold border and gold name, and the member gets a green outline over their head.
A frame flashes green when your heal lands, and red with “Too far” when the target is out of range (see Combat → Healing & support).
Frames are wider (140), long names are clipped with an ellipsis, weapon-type glyphs sit in a column to the left of the frame, and ally buffs are smaller with a thin ring.

blocks.text: Warbands (0.6.6)

items: The leader of a full party can invite a sixth person, which forms a warband: up to 25 players in 5 groups of 5. Invite with “Invite to Warband” in the player menu or “/invite Name” in chat, and the game asks you to confirm first. When the leader of another party joins, their whole party comes along.
Warband members work like a party: no damage between them, you see their health bars and compass markers, and mass heals cover the whole warband.

XP and gold from monsters are shared across the warband members nearby, but much more thinly than in a party: with 25 people each gets about 9% of what they'd get solo. Up to 5 people, party rules apply.
5×5 warband frames replace the small party frames. F1–F5 picks the group you want at hand, and Ctrl+1–5 targets players in that group.
From the player menu the leader can promote a member to leader, move them to another group or remove them. You leave a warband from the Escape menu (“Leave warband”) or the player menu.
If you disconnect, you keep your spot in the warband for 15 minutes.
Warband chat: “/wb text”.

blocks.text: Loot rolls: Need / Greed / Pass (0.6.6)

items: When a monster drops a relic of Fine quality or better, or a rare material, while you're in a party or warband, every eligible player nearby gets a roll card on the left side of the screen: Need (Y), Greed (U), Pass (P). You have 30 seconds to decide, and no answer counts as Pass.

Everyone rolls d100. Need beats Greed, and with the same choice the higher roll wins. The item goes to the winner's backpack or, if it's full, to a bag only they can pick up. The result is posted in group chat.
If everyone passes, the item stays in a bag on the ground for anyone.
Loot from killed players isn't rolled for, but every pickup from their bag is posted in your party or warband chat: who took what from whom.
The new keys can be rebound in the controls settings, under “Group targeting & loot”: the targeting modifier (Ctrl), targets 1–5, groups 1–5 (F1–F5) and Need/Greed/Pass (Y/U/P).
Holding the targeting modifier doesn't fire skills from the action bar, so Ctrl+1 picks a player instead of casting.

sections.title: Economy & Banking
sections.dek: Gold is regional, risky to carry, and painful to lose.

blocks.text: Gold loss on death

Dying drops your entire purse into the bag by your corpse. 20% is permanently lost; the remainder is a lootable entry in the loot window with Take / Take All options. This was deliberately set extreme to start, to be tuned down later if needed.
Not in your own town: a resident who dies inside their region's building area drops no loot — gear and backpack stay with them (see Building & Logistics → Resident towns).
Starter money: the Crown orders board

The Crown buys basic goods (pebbles, sticks, herbs) at fixed prices at the Crown orders board, next to the mint in the Wayfarer Village — the starter money tap. Trades between players happen player to player (Tab, click a player → Trade).
Coins from mobs (0.6.10)
Coins from mobs depend on their tier. Bandits give less than before (10–14 each), and the Forgotten give more.

The 0.6.10 notes call the bandits thug, knifeman, archer and ambusher, and name a Forgotten tracker. Elsewhere this record uses Brute, Cutthroat and Archer for bandits and Stalker for the Forgotten; the notes don't say how the names match up.
Mints & regional banking

items: Mints act as regional banks: depositing gold protects it from theft/death loss and lets you spend it at markets/crafters within that region only. Mints are not global — moving gold elsewhere means carrying it in inventory, where it's stealable again.
Ancient coins are convertible into gold via mints.

items.text: Mint Deposit/Withdraw now refreshes your account balance and purse immediately — previously this could go stale.

blocks.text: A region can build a mint from level 1 (it was level 2).
House banks
The bank belongs to the House, not the region — that's the core idea. The mint coins gold into a House bank account, and deposits/withdrawals happen at the mint.
If you own 3 regions as a House, everybody will be able to use the same bank in every of these regions.
Branches & licensing

items: A House automatically gets a branch in every region it holds — one shared account, usable at any of them. Deposit in one region, withdraw in another.

Branches aren't limited to a House's own regions: a region owner can license another House's bank to operate there too. Enough licenses and a single House's bank becomes, in practice, a global bank — even though no bank is globally guaranteed by design.
The same licensing model applies to religious Houses (churches).

blocks.text: Using an account

items: No “opening an account”: any player — House member or complete stranger — can walk up to a licensed branch and deposit or withdraw. There's no signup step.

A bank House can freeze an account. So far this has been tied to war: if your House is declared an enemy of a bank's House, your account there is frozen — and other banks can freeze your assets too, effectively letting a third party apply financial pressure on someone else's war.

blocks.text: Taxes & fees

items: Every deposit and withdrawal is taxed, and that cut is split between the bank's House and the region owner where the transaction physically happens.
The House master additionally sets the House's own transaction tax (minimum 2%); the Crown takes a flat 2% on top of that.
The Crown bank is a last resort for orphaned accounts (no House to claim them), taking a 40% cut.
Plot rent was auto-deducted from the House bank account (0.6 g/m²/day) — replaced in 0.5.0 by rent per period from your own account (see Building & Logistics).

blocks.text: Mercenary contracts: a mercenary House can be hired for a fee — no automated success verification; the hirer signs and pays, the mercenary House manually marks the job “completed” to release payment.
Region upkeep — Requisitions

items: Every week, a region posts requisitions on a board at its Obelisk: planks, oak, blocks, ingots, logs, nails — paid for out of the region's treasury.
Board deliveries are the only way to deliver resources to a region and to trigger region upgrades (via the Region Upgrade tab).
Unmet upkeep costs prestige; a region with no funds goes dormant after 14 days.
The Obelisk zone is restricted to residents of the House currently holding it.
House prestige is gained from paid upkeep, region upgrades, and member deliveries; it's only lost from negative events (unmet upkeep, an expired claim).

blocks.text: A level-2 region's upkeep runs to roughly 7,200 gold/week.

items: Weekly region upkeep depends on the plot area in the settlement plan. The number of residents no longer counts, so alts can't inflate an enemy House's costs.
Each level has a minimum area the cost starts from: 200 m² at level 1, 600 m² at level 2. The planner shows an “upkeep ~N / week” estimate for the current plan.
The week under way when 0.6.10 came out was still settled the old way; the new rates apply from the next period.

The requisition board no longer appears next to the Obelisk by itself: the rulers build it as a Civic building (see Building & Logistics → Running a settlement). Until one stands, the Obelisk takes deliveries.

blocks.text: Fixed: a region that reached level 1 in the middle of the week had no upkeep and showed “0 / 0 items delivered”. Such regions got that week's requisitions right after the 0.6.11 update.
The region treasury is secret: only officials see the balance. Everyone else, on the map too, only sees whether the region is in debt.
Bank first, purse second (0.5.0)

items: A region's bank is the bank of the House that rules it. If the region has no ruler, or the House has no mint, it's the Crown Bank.
A workshop owner's income (75% of the customer's fee) goes to their account in the region's bank, even while they're offline.

These come out of your account in the region's bank first, with the purse covering the rest: processing-table fees; workshop upgrade licence and repair; hiring, upkeep and overdue wages of hirelings; plot claim fees. Plot rent works the same way.
Hireling upkeep is paid from your account even while you're offline — before, the debt kept piling up.
The backpack shows, under the purse, the bank of the region you're standing in and your balance there; its tooltip lists all your accounts.

sections.title: Great Projects & The Chronicles
sections.dek: Where the treasury goes, and where the server's history is kept.

blocks.text: Great Projects: seven one-of-a-kind structures, one per server, funded by regional trade routes and treasuries.

The Chronicles: a permanent, server-wide historical record of what players did — including betrayals. This is the payoff of the full design chain: resources → gear → regions → trade/treasury → Great Projects → Chronicles.
Since 0.6.0 a Legendary T4 item — a Masterwork piece with a Relic — is written into its region's Chronicle (see Crafting → Relics).
Finishing one isn't “gg”

Completing all seven doesn't end the server. A Great Project can be destroyed — either by a siege whose specific objective is tearing it down, or as a side effect of the region it stands in being captured outright.
Kingdom-wide bonuses

Each of the seven Great Projects grants a different server-wide bonus to the kingdom that holds it — deliberately powerful (“OP”, in Sethan's words), which is what makes holding one worth defending and worth sieging. Examples given: higher chance of rare resource spawns, bonus damage/HP in battle, and full map visibility of every enemy army and caravan.
No seasons: the world doesn't reset or rank on a recurring cycle — the Chronicles and whatever's been built stand permanently, subject only to what other players (or the Invasion) do to them.

sections.title: Crafting, Gathering & Materials
sections.dek: Four tiers of materials, the top one only in corrupted ground; since 0.6.0 crafted gear rolls a quality and wears out.

blocks.text: Crafting, gathering, hunting, and skinning are all in and playable. Four tiers of materials — Tier 3 weapons deal x2.05 of Tier 1 damage, Tier 4 weapons deal x2.9 of Tier 1 damage.
Blight biomes & Tier 4 resources

blocks.caption: Three blighted biomes on the current map

items: The Blight is recognisable by purple air and violet crystals — stronger enemies, rarer materials.
Tier 4 resources grow only in these three biomes — the plain “Blight” decoration around the Forgotten's sites elsewhere (the old watchtowers, now the strongholds) doesn't count.

Blighted wildlife (Blight Forest & Blight Plains): wolves, stags, and does — noticeably stronger, with changed skin (grey, blotched, no fur, darker/more sinister-looking); stags fight with their antlers and charge. Skinning blighted animals yields Blight Hide (T3).
Tier 2 workshops process the four T4 resources (Mithral, Ancient Wood, Blight Fibre, Beast Hide) and require the region to be level 2.
Holding an Obelisk near a Blight biome gives a House a unique material advantage.

blocks.text: Tools & gathering

items: Pebbles, sticks and herbs lie on the ground and need no tools to pick up.
Crude tools come from stick + stone hand recipes: hatchet (wood), pickaxe (ore, stone), sickle (herbs), knife (skinning). They go in the TOOLS slots; iron tools come from the blacksmith later.
Trees, ore veins and stone deposits are shared: everyone hitting the same node works on the same progress bar.
Wolves and deer give hides, fat and bones — skin the body with a knife.
New models for the hatchet, pickaxe, sickle and skinning knife in five tiers: stone (T0), bronze (T1), iron (T2), steel (T3) and mithril (T4).
Iron, steel and mithril tools are made by the blacksmith. Better tools give a better chance at rare finds.
Tools sit properly in a closed fist instead of crossing the hand at an angle.

blocks.text: Processors vs crafters

rows: Workshop stations in the village, worked by NPCs: sawmill, mason, smelter, tannery, loom, drying rack
Turn raw materials into processed ones (logs → planks, ore → ingots, hides → leather) for a small Crown fee
Players at the benches: carpenter, anvil, leatherworker, tailor, alchemist
Make components and finished goods — weapons, armour, tools, potions — from processed materials

blocks.text: Workshop queues are private and keep running while you're away, up to 2 hours of work per workshop — hand in the materials, come back later. A station only works with a wayfarer assigned to it (see Wayfarers & NPC Workers).
Other notes

items: A mint exists for currency conversion/processing (see Economy & Banking).
Crafting is considered fairly solid already; crafting XP was multiplied 10x by the developer to push further testing.
Weapons have associated “spells” tied to them — a system still being tested.
Item/crafting icons were screenshots of the actual item mesh, not custom-drawn — replaced in 0.6.0 by new icons for all items, in one style (see UI / HUD).

blocks.text: The top tier of the heavy armour set (T4 chest, shoulders and belt) is now bright steel with a white and red tabard, instead of dark armour with gold trim.

items: Claim Banner: Carpenter's Bench (Carpentry 10, tier 2), from a Warden Relic and tier 2 components.
Supplies: Carpenter's Bench (Carpentry 1; Carpentry 10 since 0.6.6). Each one pays for one respawn at a claim camp.
Warden Relic: a 10% drop from the stronghold bosses, such as the Ancient Bone Warden. It replaced the Ancient Sigil in Obelisk level costs.

blocks.text: Item quality (0.6.0)

items: Crafted weapons, armour, shields and tools roll a quality: Common, Fine, Superior or Masterwork. Each step is worth half a tier, so a Superior T1 sword hits like a Common T2 one, and a Masterwork T3 piece beats a Common T4.
Crafting no longer fails. A recipe is locked until your profession reaches its level; after that it always works, and luck goes into the quality instead.
The crafting panel shows your odds for each quality before you craft. Higher Craftsman's Focus raises them.
Every crafted item carries the crafter's name.
Components and materials are always Common, so stacks stay interchangeable for trading.
With Craftsman's Focus above 75%, stackable results have a 10% chance of one extra piece.
Recipes up to 5 levels below you give full XP, up to 10 levels below give half, older ones a tenth.

The crafting station opens like the character screen: the station on the left, your backpack on the right, the world dimmed behind. A progress bar fills up and flashes when a piece is done, and a reveal plate shows the result, with sparks and a sound that grow with the quality.
Quality and durability stay with the item when you trade it, carry it in the cart, drop and pick it up, or lose it in a death bag.
Items you owned before 0.6.0 count as Common quality at full durability.
The quality reveal plays right in the recipe view at the station, not on a separate panel: the Rose heart stays where it was, and the result appears next to it.
Item icons in the crafting window keep their shape — ingots are no longer squeezed into squares.
The “+” in the relic slot sits in the middle of the slot.

Quality now shows on light armour with small stats, like the Outcast set. A Fine or Superior piece used to have the same numbers as a Common one; tooltips and the character card now show one decimal where needed, and the bonus counts in combat.

Crafting station: the XP shown matches what you get, including learning mode and Focus. Materials are shown times the chosen amount, recipes above your level are listed with a padlock and the level you need, Focus gives a chance for +1 item on stackable goods, and the queue bar lets you remove a single order or cancel all.
Processing: “All” means everything you can afford, and “Collect ready” works when an order is only partly done.
New names: Iron and Steel Longsword, Iron and Steel Zweihander.

blocks.text: Tier 0 & quality caps (0.6.8)

items: Tier 0 is for starter items: the Castaway set and the wooden training swords. Their tooltip says “Tier 0 (starter)”.
New starter weapons: a one-handed Wooden Training Sword and a two-handed Wooden Training Longsword. Craft them by hand (Woodworking 1) from sticks and a scrap of cloth for the grip.
New characters start in a Castaway tunic and shorts, given once when you pick your starting village.

blocks.text: The crafting odds panel shows the cap (“this tier caps at …”). Items crafted earlier are not changed.

A Legendary item is a Masterwork piece with a Relic, so Legendary now starts at T2. The 0.6.7 notes also call the stone tools T0; the 0.6.8 notes name only the Castaway set and the wooden swords as Tier 0 starter items.
Durability & repair (0.6.0)

items: Weapons wear with every hit you land, armour and shields with every hit you take, and tools with every gathering strike. Dying costs 25% durability on everything you wear.
A broken item does nothing until repaired: a broken weapon deals no damage, broken armour gives no protection, a broken tool can't gather.
Repair at the station that makes the item, for a part of its recipe. Better items can be repaired more times (1 + quality level).
A broken item with no repairs left can be recycled at the station: you get back about 40% of the raw materials one step down, never finished parts.
Durability shows as a thin bar on the item and in the tooltip, with a warning when something drops below 20%.

blocks.text: You can recycle any item made at a station, not only broken ones. Recycling an item that still works asks for confirmation first.
Relics (0.6.0)

items: Monsters drop Relics tied to their kind; bosses drop a random one far more often. Relics have their own quality, and a better Relic gives a stronger effect.
Put a Relic in the new relic slot at the crafting station. It adds its effect to the item and gives a second quality roll; the better roll wins.
Effects: Blade and Fang give more Fervor and more damage, the Pearl faster Lumen regeneration, the Signet more physical protection.
A Masterwork item with a Relic becomes Legendary. A Legendary T4 item is written into the region's Chronicle.
With Combat Focus above 75%, a kill has a 5% chance for an extra rare drop (gems, silver ore).

blocks.text: The 0.6.0 notes don't say how these Relics relate to the Warden Relic (0.5.0), which stronghold bosses drop for Claim Banners and Obelisk levels.
Armour & tiers (0.6.0)

items: Light, medium and heavy sets change shape from tier to tier — more pieces, richer parts, an extra layer at T4 — instead of getting a colour filter. T4 metal is mithril.
Shoulder pieces are now part of the chest piece; there's no separate shoulder slot.
The medium set has a leather jerkin underneath, and no armour piece leaves holes in the body any more.
The cross symbols on the Healer set are replaced with Stillmarch marks.
Materials have tiers too: copper, tin and bronze T1, iron T2, steel T3, mithril T4 (spelled Mithral in older sources), and woods and hides likewise.
The steps between tiers are now even: T2 and T3 armour give about 4–5% less protection and HP bonus; weapon damage barely changes.

sections.title: Wayfarers & NPC Workers
sections.dek: Hired NPC workers that staff the stations and bring life to the cities.

items: Wayfarers are player-owned NPC workers: you hire them to work for you. They belong to the player, not the House.
Hiring is a button in the hiring window (the cheatsheet's J key opens the Wayfarer roster).
2 per player by default; there will be ways to increase that (not detailed yet).
A wayfarer works a crafting/processing station — without one the station doesn't work. You still queue up resources yourself (e.g. ores in a smelter) and can do anything else while the queue runs.
Sethan's comparison: no different from a Pax Dei smelter, except that instead of coal you provide gold.

blocks.text: Region NPCs are a separate kind: NPCs tied to the region itself, such as NPC guards, which will also be hired.
Why they exist: to bring life to the cities and the game, avoiding the barren-wasteland feel of most Pax Dei cities.

Wayfarers only get medieval hairstyles — women's styles for women, men's for men. Styles that were only short stubble were removed, since they couldn't be displayed properly; a character with a removed style gets a different allowed one.
Wayfarers' hair and beards stay on their heads when they bend over.
Ideas that were turned down

items: House-owned wayfarers (Scratch): since villages are ruled by Houses, wayfarers could belong to the House — something it grinds for and shows off its wealth with. Declined: plots in a village don't have to be House-owned; anyone can become a citizen and rent a plot.

Unlocking wayfarers in the open world, Conan Exiles–style (Scratch): free prisoners from low-level NPC camps to add them to the hiring window. Declined — “there's like a million games with npc workers”; hiring stays a button in the window.

blocks.text: Pitch: levelled House wayfarers

Scratch's follow-up pitch, after the House-owned idea was declined: keep wayfarers a House thing, so they show which Houses are active rather than which players (“look, these guys have a lvl 4 wayfarer”). Instead of being required to run a station, a wayfarer's level would unlock recipe tiers — a forge with no wayfarer makes white gear, a lvl 1 wayfarer adds green, lvl 2 green and blue, and so on up to gold. Wayfarers would be found in the open world as an exploration reward: lvl 1 in small camps all over the world, lvl 2 in elite camps, lvl 3 in dungeons, lvl 4 in raids — possibly a grind for trader Houses to take on PvE and dungeons. No response from Sethan beyond the lore correction below.
Wayfarers aren't found in the Stillness: they're the same people as you, coming back to the continent — just House-less (Sethan, correcting the pitch's lore angle).

sections.title: Building & Logistics
sections.dek: The settlement planner, plots, protected ground, and a grid-based fight for inventory space.

blocks.text: Building on claimed land: plots and rent.
Plot rent was 0.6 gold/m²/day, auto-deducted from the House bank account — replaced in 0.5.0 (see Plots & rent below).
Plots & rent (0.5.0)

items: Plots are generated from the settlement plan and update with every change to districts and roads. Manually moving boundaries, removing plots and re-splitting are gone.
A plot keeps its number with its land: when a settlement grows, leases and buildings stay where they are.
The regional road built into the terrain counts as a town street, so plots line up along it too.
The residential and production zones are merged into one: Town.
Plot sizes: at least 12 m of frontage, at least 6 m on every side, at least 80 m².

Layout fixes: only the part of a street inside a district is split, so no plots straddle the district border; a block between two parallel streets is split in half (before, the second street got no plots on that side); plots no longer overlap at crossings or on bends.
Rent is 50 grains per m² per period, paid even while you're offline — first from your bank account, then from your purse.
Overdue rent blocks building on the plot; after 7 unpaid periods the plot goes back to the region.
You can prepay up to 30 periods. The plot window has “Pay 1”, “Pay 7” and “Release”.

blocks.text: Settlement planner
A settlement is drawn, not placed plot by plot. You draw the zones and the roads, and the plots appear on their own.

items: Drawing works like spline points: put points down, and once you connect them they become an area. You can move the points later to change the area's shape and size.
Roads are drawn the same way, but a road doesn't have to be connected back into a loop.
The middle is a predefined Civic zone around the Obelisk. Civic buildings, such as the bank or the church, go on Civic zones.
The regional roads show in the planner and can't be deleted.
The land limit grows with each region level.
Plots need a minimum area.
Residents see the plots in the Obelisk window and can rent one.
The region's ruler can evict someone from their plot with a 72-hour warning, at the cost of House prestige.
Planner 2.0: plots form a ring around the square and come in three sizes per district — small 8×16 m, medium 12×28 m and large 20×40 m.
Each shape can have rounded or straight edges, for square towns and straight streets.
The planner shows where the wall will stand (2 m out from the plots, smoothed) and where the gates go: on every road that crosses the wall.
The plan is drawn as vector art, with smooth lines and readable labels. Plots show their numbers; hover one for its size, status, rent and income.
The building panel is wider, with bigger tiles. Outside a settlement in a claimed region, the game tells you what to pay in at the Obelisk to found one.

Minimum district size: 20 × 30 m, and never narrower than 20 m. The planner rejects a smaller shape when you close it or drag a corner; the message shows the size, and the shape stays so you can fix it. The server rejects such plans too, so tiny “dots” can no longer act as walls.
Districts placed apart from each other (“several towns” around one Obelisk) stay, and each gets its own wall (see Territory Control → Walls).
Fixed: after a region levelled up, the planner sent the plan on the old grid and the server rejected every plan as “Corrupt settlement sketch”. The plan now moves to the new level's grid.

blocks.text: Sethan put the minimum plot area at “around 120 m²” from memory. The 0.5.0 notes say at least 80 m² (Plots & rent above); since 0.6.8 the smallest plot is 8×16 m, or 128 m².
The planner carries the 0.5.0 badge because the 0.5.0 notes are the first to describe plots generated from the settlement plan's districts and roads. It may have been in earlier.

Why draw it: Sethan saw how hard city planning is in Pax Dei. People have to agree to give up their plots, everything has to connect perfectly, some plots are wasted on roads and bridges, and sometimes someone builds their own little cobblestone airport in the middle of town. In Stillmarch, planning goes to a House's architects, as most big Pax Dei clans do anyway: a House can appoint a Castellan to run the region. It's less free than Pax Dei, where you put down plots and do whatever, but it lets a House set a city layout with roads and Civic zones, without the game predefining it.
Beautiful cities will be one of the main endgame activities I believe.
blocks.cite: Sethan, on why every region should look different

blocks.text: Scratch would have been fine with fixed-size plots, with the House managing who gets access. Sethan kept free drawing, since it leaves more room for unique cities.
Farming zones are planned for later, outside the walls. You'll draw the farming areas and they'll be split into plots that residents can rent, to plant any crops they want.
Running a settlement (0.5.0)

items: The Castellan's Table: a new building piece in the Civic district, one per settlement, built by the settlement's rulers. Its window is for officials only: treasury, projects, land, people.
Taking a plot back gives the tenant 3 days' notice and costs the House prestige.
Expelling a resident gives them 72 h and costs 10 prestige.

blocks.text: Wall gates no longer close by themselves while settlement raids are disabled (the current QA setting).
After claiming a region you can place the Castellan's Table and assign plots again. A new region starts with a basic town plan (civic core and roads) instead of none.

items: You can't build on roads anymore, rulers included.

The requisition board no longer appears next to the Obelisk by itself. It's a Civic building that the settlement's rulers place in build mode, up to 4 per region. Until one is built, the Obelisk takes deliveries.
The mint is available from region level 1 (it was level 2).

Becoming a City (level 3) requires the Castellan's Table (town hall), a bank (mint) and a finished palisade. The region window and the Castellan's Table list what's built and what's missing. A breach in the wall or a demolished building doesn't take a level away.
Weekly upkeep follows the plot area in the plan, not the number of residents (see Economy & Banking → Region upkeep).
The Castellan's Table has props: candlesticks, books, a scroll, papers, an inkwell, coin purses and a goblet.

blocks.text: Project sites & the region storehouse (0.6.11)

items: The Settlement Planner has a Projects section. The first project is a storehouse site in three sizes: Small 6 × 6 m, Medium 9 × 9 m and Large 12 × 12 m.
A site goes in the Civic district with its front on a road, touching it for at least 3 m. Click next to a road and the site turns to face it and moves up to its edge.
Sites can be dragged; Alt + click or the eraser removes one. A site in the wrong place shows red, and the hint says why. A plan holds up to 8 sites.
Once the plan is approved, a storehouse appears on the site: an open yard with sleepers and corner posts. It works from region level 1.
Goods pile up on the storehouse by kind: logs, planks, stone blocks, crates of metal and sacks. The stock is shared by the whole region, so every storehouse shows the same piles.
The site clears itself of grass and trees. Nobody can place their own pieces on a site; the settlement builds there.
The storehouse window [F] shows its capacity, e.g. “Storage 260 / 500”.
When the stock is full, the Baron's orders and deliveries for new walls wait. Upkeep and repairs are always taken, and goods set aside for upkeep don't take up room.
Walls and repairs use up the delivered materials. Until 0.6.11 they stayed in the stock for good.
The settlement plan can't be changed during a siege, the same as building (see Territory Control → Walls).

blocks.text: Resident towns (0.6.8)

items: Dying in your own town — as a resident, inside your region's building area — drops no loot: your gear and backpack stay with you. PvP still works there.
Obelisk sanctuary: within 12 m of the Obelisk, residents take no PvP damage. It switches off while the Obelisk is under attack.
The region HUD shows SAFE ZONE in the sanctuary and NO LOOT in your own town.

blocks.text: Build mode (0.5.0)

items: The piece catalogue sits in the left column, with a status badge under the compass and a subtler grid.
The ghost piece follows your crosshair, and LMB and RMB no longer swing your weapon.
Every refusal tells you why.
Ruler rights work in every region — before, the client always asked about the first Obelisk.

blocks.text: Build mode (0.6.9)

items: Foundations can be sunk into the ground until 25 cm of the top is left, other pieces up to 60 cm. A piece in the air turns red with “Nothing to rest on”. Before, a sunken foundation was refused and a piece above the ground showed green.
You can build right on the edge of your plot, face against your neighbour's, also rotated 180° and 270°. Snapping to the plot edge fits a piece from corner to corner.
The plot sign no longer shows on your own plot. Plot management is in the Obelisk window (Plots tab), where you also pay overdue rent.
Alt or Ctrl + mouse wheel only changes the piece's height and no longer zooms the camera.
With the catalogue open, holding RMB turns the camera while the ghost stays put.
Stations such as the smelter sit on their base instead of sinking into the ground up to the chimney.
“Someone is standing there” shows on the ghost right away. Before, it was green and only the server refused.
The smelter worker at a player's smelter stands by the coal, as at the Crown smelter (the new spot takes effect after a restart or reassignment).

blocks.text: Build mode (0.6.10)

items: A piece keeps its rotation when you move the camera and after you place the previous one. The direction is set once when you open build mode; after that, R or Ctrl + wheel turns it. The new T key turns the piece to face the camera (Shift snaps to 15°). Next to another piece, rotation lines up with its axis.
Roofs are easier to close: a slope snaps to a slope, turned around past the ridge, and ridge pieces sit on top of the slopes.
The top of the screen shows the build mode keys (rotate, T, snap mode, free placement, height, catalogue, undo), also while the catalogue is open.

Workshop and crafting tables, the mint and the Castellan's Table always stand on the ground instead of floating or sinking. On very uneven ground (more than 60 cm under the table) placement is refused with “too uneven”.
Plot and settlement borders are a misty, see-through curtain that fades upwards. The red and blue ground fill is gone.
Building and demolition are frozen from 24 hours before a region's attack window until the siege is resolved (see Territory Control → Walls).

blocks.text: Build mode (0.6.11)

items: Walls and roofs no longer hover a few centimetres above the piece below: each floor sits on the module lines, and a row of walls no longer drifts away from the floors.
A piece on the ground rests its lowest corner on the terrain. A piece with a corner hanging in the air is refused (“one end hangs in the air”).
Ctrl + wheel turns the piece by 15°, R and Shift + Ctrl + wheel by 90°; both are in the key legend. Alt + wheel changes the height in 10 cm steps (Shift + Alt + wheel: 50 cm).

Pieces snap every 1 m, a third of a module, along walls and on top of foundations. You can butt a wall against another at a third of its length, or put a post on a foundation every metre. A longer piece can also rest on a shorter one, like a beam on a post.
Z picks which point of the piece lands on the line under the crosshair: the middle, one end or the other. The status line shows the current choice.
A roof placed on a wall sits with its eave on the wall, and R picks which side the roof goes.
New pieces: beams (1, 2 and 3 m), posts (1 and 2 m), stone stairs (1, 2 and 3 m) and stone foundations (1 and 2 m).

Fixed: R turns the piece in place, with its middle under the crosshair and the grid catching its corner; before, the piece jumped to the other side of the crosshair. T (face camera) no longer plays the “denied” sound — the same key was also looking for the next ally.

blocks.text: The mouse wheel keys changed over three patches: in 0.6.9 Alt or Ctrl + wheel changed the height, 0.6.10 gave Ctrl + wheel to rotation, and since 0.6.11 Alt + wheel sets the height and Ctrl + wheel turns the piece by 15°.
Resource protection inside build boundaries

Nothing respawns inside a region's build boundary — gathered trees, mined ore, and killed animals do not come back inside the circle where zones can be painted. Living animals and standing (ungathered) trees are left alone. The boundary radius scales with Obelisk level.

Roads in the zone planner: the built-in road always counts as a road (same treatment as the forced core zone around the Obelisk), so the Obelisk can't be walled off using the road as a loophole; roads also don't count against a village's maximum size.
Inventory

items: Grid-based with variable item sizes (Path of Exile–style) — a deliberate design choice, not a weight system, meant to make inventory space itself a form of economic scarcity so one player can't solo-haul unlimited rare resources.
A weight-based alternative was proposed and rejected — exploitable (e.g. one cart hauling multiple “overencumbered” players, jokingly nicknamed the “Stillmarch Taxi Service”).

blocks.text: Item sizes & stacks (0.5.0)

Item sizes and stack sizes now come from one rule based on an item's value, instead of being set by eye. When you log in, your backpack is fitted to the new rules; anything that doesn't fit lies in a bag at your feet that only you can see and open. Nothing is lost.

blocks.caption: Stack sizes (0.5.0)
rows: 50 in the backpack; the quiver is a separate container for 200

blocks.text: Hand cart: implemented, used for hauling large quantities of materials.
The cart carries bundles, so processed goods are worth hauling further than raw ones. Cart load comes from the cargo's weight: a full cart of stone is over 100% and stops on a steep slope.
Private storage (0.6.1)

items: The chest by the order board in the Wayfarer Village is your private storage. Each chest keeps its own contents for every player: what you put in one chest stays in that chest — items don't travel between chests.

The grid and stacking work like the cart: 80 cells to start, and 4 upgrades up to 240 cells, for 50 Marks, then 2, 8 and 32 Crowns. The cost comes from your bank first, and the coin is spent for good.
The grid in the storage and cart windows now looks like the backpack.

blocks.text: In 0.6.1 the chest was missing from the world. Since 0.6.5 it stands next to the Crown Orders board (the wooden board with a roof) in Highmoor, Firstlanding and Fernhollow.
In the Wayfarer Village the chest now stands next to the order board instead of in front of it on the road. Stored items are kept.
The 0.6.1 notes price the upgrades in Marks and Crowns — coin names that appear nowhere else in this record, which otherwise speaks of gold (and grains, for plot rent).
Caravans are planned for later — larger-scale transport, and the supply-line mechanic for sieges.

sections.title: Territory Control: Obelisks & Sieges
sections.dek: Claiming dormant Obelisks is in since 0.5.0, and settlements have walls; sieges are still to come.

blocks.text: Obelisks are the core territorial control points. At the time of the DM conversation this system was barely tested, and taking land by force was the next major system on the roadmap. 0.5.0 shipped the first piece: a House can claim a dormant Obelisk (below).
