The notes only cover dormant Obelisks — taking a region another House holds isn't described yet.
Fixed, action.19: false “Move closer to the Obelisk” errors on activation, deposits, and settling are fixed — activation range is properly 12 m, measured on the ground plane, plus server-side slack.
The Obelisk (0.6.10)

Obelisks have a new model: a relay of the Network built by Perpetua. A slender slate shaft made of four pillars, with cold Network light glowing in the gaps between them, a node chamber at about 9 m and a cut capstone floating above it. The old monolith with the sun is gone. The Obelisk stands on its own round, graduated platform; the stone slabs around it are gone.

blocks.caption: The Obelisk grows with the region level (0.6.10)
rows: Bare shaft; the capstone lies at its foot
A graduated ring; the capstone floats above the shaft
A meander on the platform and gold fittings; the capstone floats higher
Four pylons on the diagonals, an armillary sphere and a halo above the capstone

items: The gaps and the chamber glow brighter with each level. An Obelisk that hasn't been activated stays dark.
The streak around the shaft and the sparks from the chamber are the cold colour of the Network. They used to be orange, with smoke.

blocks.text: The top of the pedestal no longer flickers: its pewter band was smooth enough to pick up a noisy reflection of the glowing shaft right above it, and it's matte now.
Claiming a dormant Obelisk (0.5.0)
A House can claim a dormant Obelisk and make its region the House's own. The claim is a 15-minute fight for a 20 m ring around the House's Claim Banner.

items: You need a Claim Banner, crafted at the Carpenter's Bench (Carpentry 10, tier 2) from a Warden Relic and tier 2 components. The Warden Relic drops 10% of the time from stronghold bosses such as the Ancient Bone Warden.

The House leader starts the claim in the dormant Obelisk's window. It shows the region's name, the requirements with check marks (House leader, Claim Banner in your backpack), the rules and a big claim button.
The banner stands next to the Obelisk with a 20 m ring around it, drawn on the ground like an attack telegraph in a different colour. Instead of hit points it has a 0–100% control bar.

blocks.caption: Who's in the ring decides control
rows: Drains — to zero in 90 s, faster with more enemies. At 0% the banner falls.
Refills; a fallen banner rises again, so you can retake it until the window closes

blocks.text: Enemies are players outside your House and its allies, or Blight mobs.
Winning, losing, abandoning

items: You need 15 minutes of the banner standing, within a 30-minute window. There's no overtime: the claim succeeds the moment progress reaches 15:00, and the region becomes your House's, keeping its name.
The claim fails right away if less time is left in the window than progress is missing, or if the banner lies down for more than 5 minutes straight.
The House leader can abandon the claim (“Abandon the claim” in the Obelisk window, with confirmation). The banner is lost and unused Supplies come back.
Claiming unowned land is partial loot for both sides.

blocks.text: Camp, respawns & Supplies

items: Claim camp: a tent with your House standard about 120 m from the banner, behind the House leader.

Respawning is your choice. After dying nearby a panel offers “Rise at the claim camp” (a wave every 60 s, 5 s of protection until you strike) or a normal return to the settlement or graveyard. Nobody is dropped back under the blade automatically.

Supplies (Carpenter's Bench, Carpentry 1 — Carpentry 10 since 0.6.6): 1 Supplies = 1 camp respawn, up to 20. They're taken from the House leader's backpack and their cart parked nearby when the banner goes up.

blocks.text: Blight waves & announcements

items: The first Blight wave came after 2 minutes, then one every 3 minutes (changed in 0.5.3 and back again in 0.6.6, below), each announced by purple mist 10 s before. The last wave is bigger and has an elite. Blight mobs in the ring drain control too.
Everyone in the region sees and hears the claim: an on-screen announcement with drums when the banner goes up, falls, rises again, holds or fails, plus chat reminders and a marker on the world map.
Progress shows in the event HUD — an event card on the right and a control bar at the top (see UI / HUD).
After a successful claim the banner disappears shortly after; a fallen banner fades out instead of lying on the ground.
Fewer monsters per wave: 2 + 1 per party member, up to 8 (was 3 + 2 per member, up to 14). A party of four now faces 6 per wave instead of 11.
The first wave arrives after 2:30 (was 2:00), then every 3:30 (was every 3:00). A claim's defence now has 3 regular waves and the final one, instead of 4 and the final.
Forgotten Servants in the waves attack with a proper swing in melee range. Before, some of their hits landed from a distance with no attacker.
Waves arrive in groups instead of all at once, so the server and your game stutter less when a wave starts.

blocks.text: Claim hours, fortifications & banners (0.6.6)

items: Claims are only possible between 16:30 and 22:30 Central European Time, and the last banner can be placed at 22:00. The Obelisk window shows the hours and a countdown to the opening.
Blight waves come more often again: the first after 2 minutes, then every 3 minutes.

New fortifications from the carpenter's workshop: Spiked Barricade (Carpentry 10) and Mantlet (Carpentry 11), tier T2. Place them with RMB from your backpack at the edge of the claim circle (anywhere inside it since 0.6.7). They have their own health and disappear when the claim ends. A wave that can't reach the circle breaks the fortifications together.

The banner cloth has folds and looks like canvas: weave, stains, a dirtier bottom edge, a shadow under the crossbar and light shining through. Its colours are much stronger and it slowly sways in the wind.

blocks.text: The levels match the Carpentry levels of the Claim Banner and Supplies recipes. The 0.6.6 notes don't say what the Raid, Takeover, Assault and Sabotage banners do yet.
Fortifications (Spiked Barricade, Mantlet) can be placed anywhere inside the claim circle, not only near its edge. Keep 3 m away from the banner.

The claim has the shape of the planned v1 siege below — an open-field fight for a point, with Supplies paying for respawns — but it's started by a House leader with a Claim Banner, not by an Army with a Siege Banner.
Planned siege process

items: An attacking House crafts a Siege Banner.
The banner is placed in the attacker's own region, an allied region, or a starter village (if the House holds no region).
Players join the Army by interacting with the placed banner.
The banner's owner activates it once ready, officially forming the Army.
The Army travels to the target region to attempt the siege.

blocks.text: Army formation has since taken shape in development — roles, reward budgets and mercenary pay are now visible in the House window's Army tab. See Armies & Campaigns.

items: Sieges only happen during a siege window — each region sets its own attackable window.
Each siege runs in its own separate game instance, to avoid the large-scale lag Sethan observed in Pax Dei.
The attacking Army must complete objectives (e.g. capture and hold points) to advance; success hands the region to the Army's leader.
Version 1 / MVP plan: a simple open-field “king of the hill” fight — no walls, no siege weapons — purely to validate the core loop. Fortifications and siege weapons come later.

Army supplies: each player death deducts a fixed amount; supplies are resupplied mid-siege via caravans from the controlling region (v1: craft “Supplies,” load on a cart, travel to the Army); destroying enemy supply caravans is a valid strategy. Defending regions use the same system with a baseline city bonus.
Max players per siege instance: undecided — a hard cap, or a flank system (separate sub-instances per flank, choosable respawn point) are both under consideration.

A siege's objective doesn't have to be capturing the region: it can instead target a Great Project standing there for outright destruction (see Great Projects & The Chronicles). Capturing the region destroys any Great Project in it as a side effect either way.

blocks.text: Walls

items: The game builds a settlement's walls itself, from prefabs, along the border of the drawn settlement, on the outside of the Town zone, with gates where roads cross it (see the settlement planner in Building & Logistics).
Walls expand and shrink with the shape and size of the settlement.

blocks.text: The settlement planner shows where the wall will stand, 2 m out from the plots and smoothed, with a gate on every road that crosses it (see Building & Logistics).

items: Every district gets its own wall. Districts placed apart from each other (“several towns” around one Obelisk) are walled separately; before, only the core got a wall, with wall fragments and gates in the middle of the outer districts.
Two districts split by a street narrower than 16 m count as one town: the wall runs straight across the street, with no narrow corridors.
The wall only follows the outer edge of the settlement. Holes in the town and rings of districts around the Obelisk no longer get extra layers of wall.
A gate goes where a road crosses the wall. A district without a road gets a postern facing the Obelisk.
Districts smaller than 20 × 30 m are refused, so tiny districts can no longer act as walls (see Building & Logistics → Settlement planner).

Level 1 walls are a wooden stockade with a real gate instead of the little fence, and they actually stop people: a wall section has 600 HP and the gate 1,000 HP (the fence had 300 and 500). The cost is the same.
The palisade (level 2) is the highest wall level for now. Limestone and stone walls and towers were removed, so a siege means breaking a gate.

Gates fly banners with the crest of the House that rules the region: a pair of standing banners at a stockade, banners hanging from the gate frame at a palisade. The cloth has folds, faded dye streaks and frayed edges. A region without a House shows no banners.

New battering ram: a covered frame with a hide roof and a log with an iron head hung on two pairs of ropes. It swings like a pendulum — pull back, swing, bounce off the gate — and the impact sound plays when the head hits the gate.
Building and demolition in a region are frozen from 24 hours before its attack window until the siege is resolved.

blocks.text: The settlement plan can't be changed during a siege either. Otherwise a new plan would move the walls and the breaches would disappear. Walls and repairs now use up the materials delivered to the region (see Building & Logistics → Project sites & the region storehouse).

items: For now, sieges only affect walls. Walls can be destroyed during a siege and then need rebuilding. Whether sieges will reach anything else comes later.

blocks.text: The walls carry the 0.5.3 badge because those are the first patch notes to mention them: 0.5.3 fixed wall gates closing by themselves while settlement raids are off (see Building & Logistics). They may have been in earlier.

items: Whether player buildings will be inside the siege instance isn't decided yet.
The first playtest won't have a siege instance: it would be a separate server instance, which costs money, and 100 players isn't that many yet.

blocks.text: Siege Banners were already implemented as of the DM conversation; Army formation and dynamic instance creation were the remaining MVP work. Still on the roadmap: raids for loot, Obelisk assaults, capture banners, Houses actually losing regions, then real baronies/kingdoms with alliances, elections, and casus belli.

sections.title: Armies & Campaigns
sections.dek: Pick a role, march on a campaign, get paid from the commander's treasury.

blocks.text: An army exists to prepare for and fight the instanced siege battle — but an army is still an army once the fight starts, and some of its work happens outside the instance, in the open world. An army marches only on a campaign: its commander names a target and sets aside a reward budget.
Roles

The role you pick when joining decides what you get rewarded for while the army's campaign is active. Soldiers hold the line, quartermasters carry supplies, scouts watch the roads, engineers work the siege engines.

blocks.caption: What each role is rewarded for (during the battle)
rows: Capturing objectives — fights inside the battle instance
Marking and destroying enemy caravans — operates outside the battle instance, in the open world
Paid a flat fee per attack window by the commander (e.g. 20 gold) rather than by role

items: Scouts can mark an enemy army — with a rough estimate of its size and supplies — or enemy caravans; marks appear on the map for a couple of minutes.
Role actions feed a contribution score, which determines how much each member gets paid.
Pay doesn't come from the game: the army's commander must have the money in their House's treasury.

blocks.text: The Army tab (dev build, 23 Sept)

items: The House window gained Heraldry, Diplomacy, Realm and Army tabs alongside Overview / Members / Regions / Bank.
An army entry shows its name and campaign (e.g. “Army of Straznicy Doliny · defense of Northreach Test”), its commander, where its banner was raised, and a mustering deadline (UTC).
Campaign terms are listed up front: reward budget (e.g. 50 gold), mercenary pay per attack window (e.g. 20 gold), and whether allies are welcome.
The roster counts each role (Soldier / Quartermaster / Scout / Engineer / Mercenary) and lists the Houses in the ranks; you can switch role (Serve as Soldier / Scout / Engineer) or leave the army.
“Armies of the realm” lists other armies and their state (e.g. mustering, stood down); “Raise an army” starts a new campaign.

blocks.text: Seen in a screenshot of a development build shared on 23 Sept (test region “Northreach Test”), not in a numbered patch yet. The UI is placeholder — Sethan asked for no comments on it. The systems still need testers.
Role progression (pitch)

Scratch pitched Wardogs-style progression: instead of locking you into a role, the actions you perform earn XP in matching role trees, so a character can specialize over time (e.g. engineer unlocking ladders, rams, trebuchets and archer defenses; scout getting extra map pings). Sethan found it more sandboxy in a way, but won't add skill trees for this in the near future — too much work for something only useful during sieges. Role actions still count toward the contribution score.

Wardogs comparison: it also pays you at the end of a match against what you spent on weapons and armor (a gold sink). Stillmarch is similar, but lost gear gets destroyed, and the payer is a player House, not the game.

sections.title: The Invasion
sections.dek: A recurring mini-wipe world event, roughly every 6 months.

items: High-level mob armies siege Obelisks worldwide and destroy buildings/progress there.
Structurally like a PvP siege, but the attackers are PvE (AI armies).

Destruction is partially guaranteed — armies are too numerous/powerful to fully stop — but actual damage scales with how well the server organizes its defense. Players can't defend everywhere and must choose priorities.
Anti-zerg / anti-stagnation design: disproportionately targets the largest/most dominant factions, to stop any empire from running the server uncontested and to prevent a permanent status quo.

blocks.text: Stated philosophy: the game should be unafraid to destroy player-built property/progress, unlike most MMOs. Also referenced as “the Forgotten pushing back” — part of the world eventually acting on its own, later on the roadmap.

sections.title: World Geography
sections.dek: Valdris, current playable slice: 5 km².

blocks.caption: The five regions
rows: Has its own Obelisk — near Blight Forest
Has its own Obelisk — near Blight Plains

items: Three Wayfarer villages: Firstlanding, Fernhollow and Highmoor (all three named in 0.6.5). Highmoor has a village glade with a cemetery at its edge; its nearby forest visibility was fixed in the Friday hotfixes.

items.text: Four Forgotten strongholds — Northreach, Heartland, Eastwood, Southmere — replaced the eight small watchtowers; each gate stands at the end of its road (see The Forgotten → Strongholds).
Bridges: the huge terrain ramps at both ends of every bridge are gone — the bridge slope now meets the ground.

items: Rivers, roads, day/night cycle, weather. Nights are dark: a belt lets you hang a lantern (from the blacksmith, lamp oil from the alchemist) and, for archers, a quiver.
Three Blight biomes: Blight Forest (near Heartland), Blight Plains (near Ashvale), Blight Hills (north).

items.text: Bandit camps hold men and women, including the Brute and the Cutthroat; some lie in ambush. Drowners are out there too (both named in 0.4.2).

blocks.text: 1,936 new rocks across the whole map: 574 cliffs, 853 scree piles, 385 outcrops and 124 groups of tors. Every rock sits with its base in the ground, none of them cover ore nodes, and they all have collision.
Rivers (0.6.7)

items: All four rivers meander instead of running in straight segments. The bends are irregular, some wide, some tight.
Water no longer sits above the riverbed: the water level is taken from both banks, so the “wall of water” seen from the side is gone.
Banks are gentle: shallows at the waterline, then a slope. Where a river cuts through a hill, the upper banks turn into steep gorge walls. The stepped channels with sharp edges are gone.
Old riverbeds are filled in and covered with grass or forest to match the surroundings. Riverside forest (alder, floodplain) moved with the rivers.
There's water under all six bridges and no visible steps in the riverbed. Bridges, ramps and roads stay where they were.
The western river keeps a steep cascade where it drops over a rock ledge.

blocks.text: Heartland bridge by the lake: the vertical wall of the old ditch under the span is gone, and the banks slope down to the water.
The world map (M) has been repainted: rivers follow their exact in-game course and Blight patches match the current world. Region borders are unchanged.
Swimming (0.6.7)

items: You can swim on the surface of water — no diving yet.
Swimming drains stamina. Once it runs out you lose health every second, so cross wide rivers with a full bar.
Your weapon goes on your back in the water, and abilities can't be used while swimming.
Mobs won't follow you into water. Jump into a river and they'll wait on the bank, then give up after a few seconds and head back.
Wading: from half a metre of water you slow down, to half speed at swimming depth. From 80 cm you can't sprint.
Swimmers ride the waves instead of being half the time under water and half above it.

blocks.text: Bandits & wildlife

items: In camp a sentry walks the edge of the clearing and stops to watch the forest, while the rest stay near the middle of the camp.
Out of combat bandits sheathe their weapons on their backs, and draw them when they spot you.
Bandits and animals no longer jitter in small circles on the spot — the AI kept pulling them back to their spawn point.
Bandit archers draw their bow (0.8 s) instead of shooting instantly. They spot you from range and keep their distance instead of walking up to arm's length.
Melee mobs notice you from about 10 m.
Monsters no longer slide towards you during their attack animation — they stand still from wind-up to impact.
An enemy that fled (e.g. a bandit) comes back to fight whoever chased it instead of wandering home.
An enemy returning to its spawn runs and takes no damage until it gets there — you can no longer kill it in the back on the way.
Monsters forget a player who died or moved more than 90 m away, and bleeding ends on death. No more random damage after you respawn in the village while a fight goes on at the Obelisk.

blocks.text: Bandits no longer wander the fields. They hold nine camps along the roads and keep watch from their posts. Roadside ambushes are still there.

items: Bandits wear five outfits instead of rags: Highwayman (hood with face scarf, belted jerkin), Leader (hat with half mask, brigandine, fur-trimmed cloak), Poacher (hood, vest, wool trousers with leg wraps) and two Brute sets (cheek-guard helmet, mail over a gambeson, and a fur mantle or pauldron).
The outfit goes with the bandit: Cutthroats wear the Highwayman hood or the Leader's hat, Brutes wear helmet and mail, Archers wear the Poacher hood. Every outfit has a male and a female version.

blocks.text: Bandit camps (0.6.9)

items: The roads have nine small camps instead of copies of the big camp: a tent, a campfire, two carts and a beech, with no fence. They stand where the camps stood before, with the clearing facing the road.

Each small camp has 6 bandits within about 10 m of each other, so the whole camp fights together like a full party: a Brute out front, two Cutthroats by the fire, an Archer by the carts, and a Brute and an Archer by the tent.

The big camp is one of a kind now: it stands in front of the Abandoned Chapel with the dungeon entrance. It has a new look — sharpened stakes with side gates instead of a palisade, torches, weapon racks, a brazier and a wooden ramp — and 6 bandits guard it (it used to stand empty).
Trees and bushes no longer grow through the tents: the ground is clear 20 m around the small camps and 30 m around the chapel camp. The forest around them stays.

blocks.text: Weather & sky

items: In a storm the sun and its rays disappear behind the clouds, and the sky closes over with a heavy grey layer. A full storm gets darker, with muted colours.
Lightning is one strong flash instead of flickering. Thunder follows the flash: the closer the strike, the sooner and louder it comes.
You only see and hear strikes within about 1.4 km — about two a minute, each with its thunder. The huge bright rectangle that covered the screen on a close strike is gone.
Overcast skies are grey instead of blue or navy, and rain no longer tints the world blue.
Trees, bushes and grass clearly sway in the wind, and a storm whips them harder than normal wind does.
The thick violet haze is back over the Blight, strongholds included.
The crack in the moon is see-through, showing the sky behind it.
In sunny weather you can clearly see and hear the wind: grass and trees keep swaying, and gusts roll across the meadows.
When it clouds over the wind picks up, and the harder it rains, the stronger the gale. In a downpour trees and grass bend in the wind.

blocks.text: Grass follows the wind gusts: it moves gently between gusts, and leans and ripples clearly when you hear one. Less frame-to-frame jitter.

items: At dawn and dusk the ground is no longer brighter than at noon.
Grass no longer jumps every third of a second.
Forests have ground mist under the trees in the daytime, and denser fog between them.

blocks.caption: Grass draw distance by graphics quality (0.4.2)
rows: Twice as far — about 70–120 m (was 35–60 m)

blocks.text: Grass reaches far enough that you no longer see where it ends, and vegetation keeps its detail further out.
Grass on new terrain is built in the background and no longer freezes the frame; the long draw distance on Epic stays (see Development & Testing → Performance).

sections.title: Dungeons & Raids
sections.dek: The Old Mine, under the Abandoned Chapel, is open to explore; instanced dungeons, raids and the Spire, plus world bosses and raids on settlements, are on the way.

blocks.text: In the game now

The Old Mine, a dungeon built by Lucyphere: a chapel, mine tunnels, a labyrinth and a great hall. It replaced the previous dungeon and its boss in 0.4.2, and you enter through the same portal as before. For now it's empty — no enemies, boss or chests; it's there to explore.

Rebuilt in 0.5.0: beams, pillars and planks in the first part, tunnel supports, a bandit chamber lit by torches, and patched holes. The entrance is now an abandoned chapel by the forest road (“Abandoned Chapel” on the map) with no trees growing inside, and the portal in the passage behind the statue has a visible swirl. Leaving the dungeon puts you in the middle of the nave, facing the way out.
The chapel with the dungeon entrance sits 1.8 m lower in the ground. Coming back from the dungeon puts you in the same spot as before.
Daylight no longer gets into the dungeon.
More stones, fixed rock heights and a filled-out boss room. There's a small bandit camp at the dungeon entrance.
The dungeon can only be entered solo or in a regular party. Warbands are refused — raids for large groups come later.

Interior fixes: more rocks, none floating or sunk into the floor, and the gaps in the boss room are filled. Entering through the chapel portal and coming back work as before. The bandit camp in front of the chapel now has 6 bandits (see World Geography → Bandit camps).

The 0.5.0 notes give dungeon bosses a health bar but don't say whether The Old Mine has enemies or a boss yet — “empty” is as of 0.4.2. The 0.6.9 notes say there are still no monsters or chests inside.
Instanced

items.text: 5-man dungeons — closed instances.
Cursed Dungeons — PvPvE variants of the same 5-man dungeons, with different loot.
20–25-man raids — closed instances.
The Spire — closed-instance challenges that climb floor by floor. Each floor sets its own format: solo, 5-man, 20-man or PvPvE.

blocks.text: Open world

items.text: World bosses with randomized spawns — nothing on the map marks where they are.
PvE raids on settlements (see also The Invasion).

blocks.text: Source: the dev team's PvE content list, 5 Oct 2026. Raids were previously listed as 20-man.

sections.title: Bounty / Justice System
sections.dek: Proposed, explicitly deferred — possibly to 1.0.

blocks.text: Nothing in this section is implemented. It's recorded here as a design idea floated in conversation and explicitly deferred.

items: Victim of an attack chooses: duel to the death, or flee. Escaping into a village without dying lets them report the attacker to that city's public Bounty List.
Other players can pick up a bounty as a personal contract for a reward (type undecided).
Nameplates would only flag players who are actually on a bounty list.
Limited active reports per victim; exceeding it applies a “coward” debuff to discourage spam.
Bounties must be self-funded by whoever places them, to keep them tied to genuine motivation.
Intended to drive roleplay/drama; possible “Bounty Hunter”-style achievements floated.

items: Other players' armour no longer stretches when they are far away or when your view distance is set lower.

If something was built or placed where you logged out (a wall, a claim banner, another player), you could log back in without a character — just the sky and the default interface. You now appear right next to that spot.

blocks.text: There are no patch notes here for 0.6.2–0.6.4: the 0.6.5 notes list the changes since 0.6.1.

Update required (client + server); characters, items, Houses, regions and bank accounts carry over. Changes since 0.6.0: private chest storage by the order board in the Wayfarer Village, upgradable from 80 to 240 cells; a forged-iron look for the backpack, equipment, crafting, loot, trade, cart and settings windows; the quality reveal moved into the recipe view, with new hammer-strike sounds for finished items; and smaller crafting and tooltip fixes.

Update required (client + server); characters, Houses, regions and bank accounts carry over, and items you already own count as Common quality at full durability. Update required (client + server); characters, Houses, regions and bank accounts carry over. sections.title: Development & Testing
sections.dek: Solo dev, self-hosted, tested as if it were finished.

items: Target for the small map: 20–30 concurrent players to validate core friction points; a larger map would need hundreds.
Small-map testing was expected within about a week or two of the DM conversation (20 Sept 2026).
“Forgotten Castles” — a world area/feature being brought online for testing around this time; most likely what shipped in action.20 as the four Forgotten strongholds.
Hosting: self-hosted on the developer's own PC, tunneled with an app called playit for early testing; plan is to move to Hetzner for actual alpha/playtest hosting.
Backend: server-side persistence and economy-logic tests gate every build.
Client versioning: each build requires the matching client — older clients can't connect. Characters and the database persist across builds.

blocks.text: Login names are no longer case-sensitive: “Sethan” and “sethan” are the same account.
Sign in with Steam (0.6.11)

items: Started from Steam, the game signs you in with your Steam account by itself — no account name or password to type.

The first time, you choose. BRING MY ACCOUNT: enter your playtest account's name and password once, and the account moves to your Steam account with all its characters. START A NEW ACCOUNT: a new, empty account; it takes a second click to confirm, because an older account can't be brought over afterwards.
One Steam account holds one game account. An account moved to Steam no longer signs in with a password.
Started outside Steam, the game shows the old sign-in with a password.

blocks.text: Performance (0.4.3)

The game no longer stutters as you walk through the world, especially on Epic. On the dev's test route (Epic, 6 minutes walking through meadows and forest), stutters longer than a quarter of a second dropped from almost one a minute to zero, and shorter ones (50 ms and up) from several a minute to less than one.

items: Grass on new terrain is built in the background and no longer freezes the frame.
Turning the camera quickly no longer freezes the image.
The render thread is about 40% lighter, so slower CPUs should get more FPS.
The first big memory cleanup happens under the loading screen instead of two minutes into play.
Mobs, their names and their sounds no longer weigh on the game several times a second.
Bandits coming into range appear one after another instead of all in the same frame.
A storm building up or dying down no longer reworks the sunlight every frame.

blocks.text: Video memory & graphics settings (0.5.1)
The game uses noticeably less video memory. On 12 GB cards, walking through forests on Medium, High and Epic used to overflow video memory and freeze the picture for seconds at a time.

items: The texture pool shrinks on its own when the game goes over your card's memory budget, instead of spilling into system memory.

Ray tracing covers a smaller area around you (150 m), small plants (ferns, saplings, bushes) take part in it only up to 10 m, and ray tracing data for newly loaded forest is built over several frames instead of one.
Small plants no longer feed the Lumen lighting system (the engine's lighting, not the mana resource) or its distance fields, so newly loaded forest costs less, on Medium too.
Lumen updates the lighting of newly loaded areas over more frames on Medium and High.
Leaves no longer trace their own reflections on High and Epic — they were barely visible.
On Low and Medium, and whenever hardware ray tracing is off, ray tracing is switched off completely and no longer holds memory.
New graphics option: Hardware ray tracing (On/Off). It applies with High or Epic global illumination. Turning it off frees about 1 GB of video memory and keeps everything else on your chosen preset.
A video memory readout under the preset — used / budget in GB — with a hint when you're close to the limit.

On first launch the game picks a preset for your card's memory: below 9 GB, Medium without ray tracing; below 13 GB, High. It only ever lowers the preset, once, and leaves custom settings alone. (The first-launch quality detection itself came in the Friday hotfixes — see Build & Patch History.)

blocks.text: Fewer stutters the first time you see new places: a new set of shaders, recorded on 0.5.1 across all presets and several regions, is prepared at startup. The previous set was older than the current world materials, so many shaders were still compiled during play.
Video memory saver (0.6.5)
The game uses much less video memory. Cards with 8 and 12 GB should stutter far less in forests and when you turn the camera quickly.

blocks.caption: Video memory in a dense forest at 1080p (0.6.5)

items: Interface textures are compressed (about 80 MB less), Nanite keeps a smaller geometry cache on High and lower presets, and the shadow buffers for grass no longer balloon when you turn the camera quickly.

New option in Graphics: Video memory saver. It lowers the texture budget, shadow pages, grass density, hair shadow detail and the geometry cache. It turns on by itself when video memory stays full with ray tracing already off, and from the first start on cards below 9 GB. You can switch it off any time.

Fixed a crash when ray tracing was turned off during play — lowering the preset to Medium or Low, switching ray tracing off, or the automatic switch when video memory is full. Ray tracing now turns fully off after you restart the game; the graphics window tells you when a restart is needed.

blocks.text: Server load (0.6.5)
Getting the server ready for bigger playtests:

items: The server does much less work per player: your character's animation is only calculated on the server while you attack or use a skill, monsters asleep far from everyone stop sending network updates, and when a mob is hit, only characters close to it are checked for line of sight.
Saving is spread out: one character every quarter of a second instead of everyone at once every minute, so there's no more short freeze each minute when many people are online.
Party frames send gear and looks only when they change.
Obelisk claim waves arrive in groups instead of all at once (see Territory Control).

blocks.text: Shaders & effects (0.6.7)

items: Fewer hitches the first time combat effects appear (frost, bleeding): some of them are now loaded during the loading screen.
A refreshed shader cache for every graphics preset, including combat.

blocks.text: Performance (0.6.8)

items: Fewer once-a-second micro-stutters in the forest: game systems refresh spread out over time, and gathering nodes around the player are lighter.
A refreshed shader cache, including the new outfits, swords and prompts.

blocks.text: Performance (0.6.9)
A refreshed shader cache, including the new camps, the chapel camp and the tool icons.
Performance (0.6.10)

items: A refreshed shader cache, including the new Obelisk, walls, banners, ram and border curtain.
The map HLOD — the simplified geometry you see from far away — is rebuilt.

blocks.text: Testing philosophy: testers are asked to judge the pre-alpha as a finished, final product — a practice Sethan says he learned from CD Projekt Red's QA approach on Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty and (in development) Witcher 4.
